stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted with a pulmonary embolism and started on intravenous unfractionated heparin. On day 7 her platelet count has fallen from 160,000 to 55,000/mm3, and she develops a swollen, painful calf. Her ELISA for antibodies against platelet factor 4 and heparin is strongly positive.
oneliner: 81F + PE on IV heparin + day 7 platelets 160,000 → 55,000 + new calf swelling + anti-PF4/heparin antibodies → next step?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

whyNot.A: **LMWH cross-reacts** with the antibody and keeps the platelet-activating complex going
whyNot.B: Platelets would add fuel to **thrombosis**; the problem is clotting, not bleeding
whyNot.C: Warfarin alone **depletes protein C first** and can cause venous limb gangrene before the platelets recover
whyNot.E: Any heparin dose **feeds the antibody-driven activation**; the drug must stop

answer: Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban)
why: A **fall of more than half in platelets 5 to 10 days into heparin**, with **new thrombosis** and **anti-PF4/heparin antibodies**, is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. It is **prothrombotic**, so stop **all** heparin (including flushes and LMWH) and give a **direct thrombin inhibitor** such as argatroban.

idea.rule: HIT clots rather than bleeds: stop every form of heparin and use a non-heparin anticoagulant.
also: Remove heparin flushes and heparin-coated catheters
Start warfarin only after platelets recover

stem: A 65-year-old man with long-standing hypertension is admitted with 3 days of worsening breathlessness and orthopnea. He has crackles halfway up both lungs, a third heart sound, raised jugular venous pressure and pitting leg edema. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusions. Along with intravenous diuretic, the team writes a diet order.
oneliner: 65M + long-standing HTN + 3 days dyspnea, orthopnea + crackles to mid-lung, S3, JVP up, edema → which diet order?
ask: Which of the following diet orders is most appropriate?

whyNot.A: Used in **advanced kidney or liver disease**, not to limit fluid retention
whyNot.C: Reserved for **bowel preparation or postoperative** states; offers no sodium control
whyNot.D: Helps **constipation**; does not address his volume overload
whyNot.E: Typical hospital diets carry **excess sodium**, which would keep him retaining water

why: **Orthopnea, S3, crackles, raised JVP and edema** mean volume overload from decompensated heart failure. **Sodium restriction** lowers water retention and so preload, alongside diuretics.

idea.rule: Water follows sodium, so limiting dietary sodium limits the volume that overloads a failing ventricle.
also: Loop diuretics remove sodium, and water follows
Aldosterone antagonists cut distal sodium reabsorption
A salty meal is a common trigger of decompensation
Sodium restriction also helps ascites in cirrhosis
